entry.title: [BIP Draft] Co-signer Spending Policies
entry.summary:
The current landscape of Bitcoin co-signing solutions in contexts such as lending, vaults, and escrow is fragmented. Each co-signer or service provider enforces its own proprietary rulebook, resulting in a lack of portability and auditability. Users find themselves locked into specific vendors without any standardized way to verify or migrate their policies. Incidents involving platforms like Celsius and BlockFi illustrate the risks inherent in pooled custody models, where users must place blind trust in providers rather than relying on transparent, verifiable rules.
A proposed remedy to these challenges is the introduction of Co-signer Spending Policies—an open and portable format that standardizes the description of what actions a co-signer is permitted to authorize, under what conditions, and based on which forms of evidence. This approach focuses on creating a common language for policy expression, leaving the implementation of co-signers themselves flexible and independent. Importantly, this solution does not require changes to the Bitcoin protocol, such as a soft fork.
The underlying design leverages existing Bitcoin features including Taproot outputs, Miniscript scripting, Partially Signed Bitcoin Transactions (PSBTs), MuSig2 multi-signatures, and Discreet Log Contracts (DLC) oracles. Script mechanisms enforce all feasible constraints, while human or institutional co-signers handle external requirements like price triggers or loan repayments. To ensure that funds are never irretrievably locked, there is always at least one fallback path—typically governed by a timelock—that allows recovery without needing a co-signer’s approval.
Each spending policy is uniquely identified and sets out permissible transaction outputs along with the required evidence for each scenario, such as cryptographically signed attestations of repayment or price data, along with stipulations regarding recency and finality. The co-signer reviews the PSBT and accompanying evidence against the policy before either signing the transaction or refusing it, providing an auditable record of their decision. For instance, in a lending scenario, collateral can be released upon verification of repayment, liquidated if certain price conditions are met, or reclaimed by the borrower after a defined period has elapsed.
For this initiative to achieve broad adoption and become a true standard, critical feedback on the conceptual framework is sought, particularly regarding whether the policy layer is the optimal level for standardization and identifying any structural weaknesses in the design. Further input is requested on technical questions such as the use of JSON versus TLV encoding, the mechanics of the fallback timelock, and the appropriate location for the statement format definition. Ultimately, real-world testing and independent implementations are essential. Only when two or more distinct projects demonstrate interoperability will this policy framework be recognized as a practical standard.
